questions.stem: Riya's father disagrees with the rent his landlord has charged and the landlord proposes to settle it privately between the two of them. In steps, explain what the rule of law requires in this situation, and say where that requirement is written into the Constitution.

markingPoints.description: The Rule of Law is a fundamental principle of any democratic society (1)
It ensures equality before the law and equal protection of the law (1)
Disputes are settled in a court of law through procedures established by law, not by force or personal influence (1)
No citizen is punished without following the procedure, and all get a fair chance to defend their rights (1)
The principle is enshrined in Article 21, and the rights are enforceable in courts (1)

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Step 1 — The Rule of Law is a fundamental principle of any democratic society.
Step 2 — It ensures equality before the law and equal protection of the law, and that no one is above the law.
Step 3 — So a dispute like this one is resolved in a court of law through procedures established by law, not by force or personal influence.
Step 4 — No citizen can be punished without following that procedure, and everyone is given a fair opportunity to defend their rights.
Step 5 — The principle is enshrined in Article 21, and the rights it safeguards are enforceable in courts of law.

questions.stem:
Aarav has just moved to Canada for a school exchange year. His host family explains that Canada has no president. At the top of the country stands a representative whom the Monarch appoints, and that appointment follows the advice given by the head of the government. Aarav finds it strange that someone living in another country can make this choice, so he asks his teacher whether the same arrangement exists in India and in the United Kingdom. His teacher reminds him that the three countries are grouped together under one common form of government, which is why a comparison between them is possible at all.

Answer the three questions below.
1. Name the post that the representative holds in Canada.
2. Say who makes the appointment to that post, and on whose advice it is made.
3. Aarav wonders whether Canada alone is arranged this way. Using the one form of government that Canada shares with India and the United Kingdom, explain why all three can be compared on this point.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. Governor-General. (1)
2. Appointed by the Monarch, on the advice of the Prime Minister. (2)
3. All three are Representative Democracies (Parliamentary Democracies), so their heads of state work inside the same form of government. (2)

Sarita's class is preparing a display on different heads of state, and she has been given three cards to lay out. The first card belongs to India and shows a President. The second card belongs to Canada and names a person who is not elected at all, but is appointed by the Monarch. The third card belongs to the United Kingdom and shows a Monarch, and beside it Sarita writes that the country is placed under a Constitutional Monarchy. The display supervisor then asks her to add one more line explaining why the three cards may be shown side by side.

Answer the three questions below.
1. Name the official who holds the post of head of state in India.
2. Say how that post is filled in Canada, and name the person who fills it.
3. Adding the Constitutional Monarchy note and the shared form of government, explain what the display is showing about the three countries.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. The President, the Head of State. (1)
2. The post is filled by appointment, not election; the holder is the Governor-General, appointed by the Monarch. (2)
3. All three are Representative Democracies (Parliamentary Democracies), so the same kind of government applies even though the head of state differs. (2)

questions.stem:
Ved is revising the constitutional framework before his annual test. He makes a card for each point he must remember. The first card says that India has a written constitution. The second card says that more than one political party competes for power. The third card says that authority is divided between the union and the states, and it names this Federalism. Two further cards list the Fundamental Rights and the Fundamental Duties that every citizen of India holds. Ved then meets a friend who studies Canada, where Federalism also appears, but where the power that is left over stays with the union government.

Answer the three questions below.
1. Name the type of constitution on Ved's first card.
2. Name the feature on his third card, and say between which two levels of government it divides authority.
3. Ved's friend studies Canada, which also has Federalism. Compare the two countries: what feature do they share, and how does the power that is left over compare between them?

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. A written constitution. (1)
2. Federalism, dividing authority between the union and the states. (2)
3. Both share Federalism. India's list runs to the union, the state and a concurrent list, while Canada records that the power which remains stays with the union government. (2)
